title: Fewer screens, a clearer product
excerpt: Simplify a product interface by merging steps that share a decision and cutting screens that only pass people along. What remains should show the choice.
alt: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it. The sketches are where extra screens become visible as hallways.
caption: Count the decisions, then the screens. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should two screens become one?
faqs.answer: Merge them when they ask for the same decision and the person learns nothing new between them. Keep them apart when the second step depends on seeing something new, or when the action is hard to undo and needs a clean moment of its own. A confirmation should state the consequence, not repeat the whole form.

faqs.question: Will fewer screens make the product feel limited?
faqs.answer: A clear product feels specific, which is different from feeling empty. Got Next and Leadly are public examples of interfaces built around a job and a small set of actions. The limit is the point. A screen that shows every stored field asks the person to invent the decision themselves.

faqs.question: What should we not merge?
faqs.answer: Do not fold a destructive action into a harmless screen to save a click. Do not combine steps that different people complete, such as a requester and an approver, just to shrink a diagram. Do not hide a required choice inside a default the person never sees.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
To simplify a product interface, merge steps that share a decision and remove screens that only pass a person along. A screen should exist because someone has to see something new, choose something, or confirm an action they cannot undo. A screen that exists because the database had another table is a hallway. Hallways make a product feel larger and slower without making the job clearer.

The temptation is strongest in tools that can show everything. A lead list with every column the database stores. A trading view with every control the builder uses personally. The more the first screen tries to be the whole product, the harder it is to see the decision. Got Next and Leadly, public Hanabi product interfaces, go the other way. Each is built around a job and a small set of actions. They are references for focus, not templates to copy pixel for pixel.

## Find the steps that are one decision

Write the current flow as a list of screens. Beside each, write the decision the person makes there. If two neighbors require the same decision, they are candidates to merge. Picking a person and then confirming that you picked them is often one decision with an anxious extra click. Choosing a file, and then setting options that only make sense once the file is visible, may be two decisions, because the second depends on seeing the first.

Merge when the person gains no information between the steps. Keep a separate screen when the information is large, or when the action is hard to undo and needs a quiet moment. That confirmation should name the consequence. Repeating the entire form in a second step adds a screen and no judgment.

A five-step wizard is sometimes one form that was afraid of looking tall. Try it as a single page with a visible order. If it is still understandable, the wizard was a hallway. If a step needs a different object, such as a preview that changes the choice, give that step the screen and let the others go.

## Show the choice, not the inventory

On the screen that remains, show the fields that change the decision. Secondary facts can live on the object, one click away, under a label that says what they are. A lead tool gets worse when every row tries to be the entire record. The row should answer who this is and what to do. The record can hold the history.

A trading screen has the same failure mode. Someone scanning for what changed does not need every order type drawn at full size. They need the change, the choice, and a way into detail. A first view that contains the entire toolkit teaches people to ignore half the controls. The control you add next joins the ignored half.

Nielsen Norman Group reported in 2011 that people often leave a web page within 10 to 20 seconds, and that they read only about a quarter of the text on pages they actually visit. [The research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is about web pages, and a product screen faces the same hurry. Extra panels do not get read just because you shipped them. They compete with the decision. Cutting a screen is an act of respect for the quarter of the words someone might actually see.

Got Next and Leadly are worth opening because a visitor can see a shipped interface that has already made this cut. The job is legible. The actions are few. Hanabi shows them as product work, alongside other projects, so a founder can tell focus from a sparse theme. A sparse theme with three vague buttons is still unclear. Focus means the remaining controls belong to one decision.

## A cut you can make this week

1. List the screens in the main job.
2. Write the decision each screen asks for.
3. Merge any pair that shares a decision and adds no new information.
4. On what remains, remove fields that do not change the decision.
5. Read the flow aloud. If it takes a tour to explain, it is still a tour.

Do this before you add the next feature. New features like to arrive with their own screen, and the count only goes up. Ask whether the feature is a new decision or a field on a decision you already show. A field is often the honest answer, and it keeps the map stable.

Keep a later list so a cut does not feel like losing the idea. The idea can return when the first path is finished. Six quiet screens are easier to make clear, fast, and honest in their empty states than twenty loud ones. The later list is also how you explain the cut to a cofounder who loved the extra step. The step is postponed, not insulted.

## What should stay apart

Keep a destructive action on its own moment, with the consequence written out. Folding it into a harmless screen to save a click saves the wrong thing. Keep steps apart when different people complete them. A requester and an approver are not one user who happens to click twice. Combining them to shrink a diagram hides a handoff the product needs to show.

Keep a required choice visible. A default is a decision you made for the person. If they would be surprised by it, they should see it before the action. Hiding it to reduce clutter is how clutter moves into the support inbox.

Density still belongs in some jobs. A person who lives in a tool all day can handle more on one screen than a person who visits once a month. The test is whether each visible control earns a place in the decision. A clear dense screen has a hierarchy. A sparse screen with equal weight on three vague actions does not. Count decisions, not whitespace.

## After the hallways are gone

The screens you keep are often lists and overviews people scan. A scan needs an order: what changed, what needs a person, what can wait. That order is the subject of the next piece, [designing dashboards people can scan](/blog/dashboards-people-can-scan).

Got Next, Leadly, and the rest of the public projects are collected on [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). Use them to see what a focused interface looks like when it has been built, not only framed.
